lead.headline: Why One Meeting Far Away Matters to Every Family
lead.deck: Three nuclear powers plan their first meeting together.
body: Some decisions made far away matter at every kitchen table. This week the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, the world’s biggest nuclear powers, plan to meet together for the first time ever.

US President Donald Trump stops first in Manila, in the Philippines. On Thursday, in Shenzhen, China, he is due to meet China’s Xi Jinping, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin is due to join them. They are to talk about nuclear stockpiles, the weapons each country keeps.

A White House official said no deal to get rid of the weapons is expected, and called the meeting a starting point for talks on shrinking stockpiles. China has long said America and Russia must first cut their own large arsenals before it talks about its own.
Trade touches homes too. Last year Trump and Xi agreed a truce that cut some US tariffs, taxes on goods brought in, on things from China. It runs out in January.

world.headline: Europe Sends Ukraine Its Biggest Payment and Squeezes Russia’s Banks
world.deck: EU ministers say a ceasefire, a stop to the fighting, must come first.
body: Sanctions are rules that cut off money and trade, to put pressure on a country without fighting. On Monday the European Union, a group of European countries, added 113 new names to its sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, including nearly 50 banks and other money firms. Their assets, such as money and property, are frozen, and 12 people on the list may not travel to EU countries.

EU ministers also approved nearly 8 billion euros for Ukraine, the largest single payment from a fund called the Ukraine Facility. The fund offers more than 50 billion euros until 2027. Once this payment arrives, Ukraine will have received more than 40 billion euros from it.
The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Russia keeps adding demands as an excuse to keep the war going. “A ceasefire must come first,” she wrote.

us.headline: One Faulty Box Kept America’s Planes on the Ground
us.deck: Flights are close to normal again after Friday’s stop.
body: On Friday, travellers across America waited at once. The FAA, which guides planes through the sky, stopped every flight from taking off for more than four hours. About 3,500 planes were already flying, and all of them landed safely. About 9,159 flights were cancelled that day.

The cause was a router, a box that passes messages between computers. A worker replacing one in El Dorado, Arkansas, set off a flood of about 1,000 log-on attempts every four to five seconds. Officials found no sign of a cyberattack.

By Monday most airlines were back to normal or close to it. The government has asked for more money to upgrade the old network. Officials say it is safe to fly, and advise checking with your airline before you go.
us.why: When one part of a shared system fails, thousands of family trips can be held up at once.

india.headline: Businesses in India Pay Much More for Fuel and Power
india.deck: Economists warn shoppers could feel it next.
body: Before goods reach a shop, the businesses that make and sell them buy fuel, power and materials. The prices they pay when they buy in bulk are called wholesale prices. On Monday India’s government said these were 12.29% higher in October than a year earlier.

The biggest push came from fuel and power, which cost 32.84% more. Electricity alone rose 8.06%, after falling a little in September. Economist Madan Sabnavis of Bank of Baroda pointed to higher crude oil prices and strong demand for power during heat waves. Food rose 8.58%, a little slower than the month before.

So far, companies have passed on only some of these costs. Sabnavis said the rises will push companies to raise their prices. Economists at a firm called ICRA expect October to be the peak, with about 11.6% in November. The next figures are due on 14 December.
india.why: Economists warn that what businesses pay now could show up in family shopping in the coming months.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to The Breakfast Table for Tuesday, November 17. Today: a meeting of three powerful leaders, a day when America’s planes stood still, and why businesses in India are paying more.
Let’s start with that meeting. Who is meeting, and why does it matter to us at home?

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet together for the first time ever. These are the world’s biggest nuclear powers, and the weapons they keep matter to every family on Earth.
Where is it happening?

In Shenzhen, in China, on Thursday. President Trump stops first in Manila, in the Philippines. Then China’s president, Xi Jinping, is due to meet him, and Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, is due to join them.
So will they agree to get rid of nuclear weapons?

No. A White House official said no deal to get rid of the weapons is expected, and called the meeting a starting point for talks on shrinking stockpiles, the weapons each country keeps. China has long said America and Russia must first cut their own large arsenals.
Now, planes. What happened on Friday?

The FAA, which guides planes through the sky, stopped every flight in the United States from taking off for more than four hours. About 3,500 planes were already flying, and all of them landed safely.
What went wrong?

A router, a box that passes messages between computers. A worker was replacing one in El Dorado, Arkansas. That set off a flood of log-on attempts, about 1,000 every four to five seconds. Officials found no sign of a cyberattack.
Is it fixed now?

By Monday most airlines were back to normal or close to it. The government has asked for more money to upgrade the old network. Officials say it is safe to fly, and advise checking with your airline before you go.
Last story. Why are businesses in India paying more?

Before goods reach a shop, businesses buy fuel, power and materials. The prices they pay when they buy in bulk are called wholesale prices. In October they were 12.29 percent higher than a year earlier. The biggest push came from fuel and power, which cost 32.84 percent more.
Does that mean shop prices go up too?

Maybe later. So far, companies have passed on only some of these costs. But economist Madan Sabnavis said the rises will push companies to raise their prices. Economists at a firm called ICRA expect October to be the peak.

A new router The paper says a worker replacing a router set off a flood of log-on attempts.
Which costs pushed India’s wholesale prices up the most?
Fuel and power The paper says fuel and power cost 32.84% more than a year before.
If you could ask the three leaders meeting in Shenzhen one question, what would it be?
That is The Breakfast Table for today. Thank you for listening, and have a lovely day.
